data.title: Can Binance afford to pay for the $6.3 billion theft in history's largest hack?
data.description:
Summary: At 4:20 AM on October 30th, Binance's hot wallet was emptied using an "authorization order." $5.5 billion to $6.3 billion flowed out of the blockchain, and the entire industry collectively froze approximately $3 billion. The most credible estimate of the net loss is currently just over $1 billion—seven times the amount from the Bybit case in 2025, making it the largest loss in crypto history. But after thoroughly examining Binance's assets, I want to say something counterintuitive: Binance can afford to pay this loss; financially, it's not even a serious blow. The real bill isn't on the balance sheet, but the moment the withdrawal button lit up again. This article discusses four things: how the money was stolen, how much Binance actually makes, what various parties in the crypto world were doing in those 24 hours, and what this event will ultimately change.

I. The key was never lost; the door was opened by someone from within the family

Let's clarify the events first, because the figures circulating online are very confusing.

At 4:20:59 AM Beijing time on October 30th, a new address submitted a transaction to the Binance hot wallet "Binance 14," containing 50 consecutively numbered authorizations.

Three minutes and 24 seconds later, all 167,464 ETH, 1.615 billion USDT, and 63 other tokens including UNI, LINK, and AAVE in this wallet were wiped out in a single transaction. At 4:41 AM, the attacker, using the legitimate identity of "Binance 14," directed another wallet under its name to transfer 823 million USDC in one go. By 6:40 AM, the attacker had made four rounds of sweeping purchases, even taking newly deposited cash. The money went to at least nine blockchains. Ethereum alone saw an outflow of approximately $3.3 billion, plus about $1.45 billion from Bitcoin and about $630 million from Tron, bringing the gross outflow estimates to between $5.57 billion and $6.3 billion – Binance's official figure is "a total impact of approximately $6.3 billion." CZ and Binance: Industry-wide effort to freeze funds (Image source: Deep Tide TechFlow) Here we need to pause and explain a term, because the key to the entire case lies in it: EIP-7702. This is a new feature introduced in Ethereum's upgrade last year. In short, a regular wallet can sign a "delegation form," temporarily handing over its operational authority to a piece of program code, allowing it to execute batch transfers on your behalf. The initial design intention is good—to make wallets smarter. But in the hands of hackers, this delegation form is a contract of servitude: once they trick you into signing it, they can transfer all your money without ever needing your private key again. An attacker packages 50 authorizations into Binance's hot wallet at once, essentially a shotgun-style blind shot—because they don't know the real-time sequence number of the target wallet, just one hit is enough. And it hit. Why would Binance's wallet sign such a thing? Binance's own preliminary investigation stated: a development and operations engineer's laptop was compromised, allowing the attacker to access the service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. In other words, the private key never left Binance—two hours after the incident, the Binance security team even used the same private key to salvage the remaining assets in the wallet. What was lost wasn't the key, but the judgment capability of the signature system. A compromised laptop: the starting point of this incident (Image source: The Paper) This wasn't a spur-of-the-moment decision. On-chain replays show that the attackers began preparing on October 28th, rehearsing the entire process twice with a test wallet, with the final rehearsal only three and a half hours before the actual attack. Even more worthy of further investigation is: why would a hot wallet from an exchange with the highest global security level issue such a clearly abnormal delegation? On-chain researchers later pointed out at least three defensive flaws. First, the authorization of 50 consecutive serial numbers in one package was an extreme anomaly that should have been blocked by risk control, but it passed smoothly. Second, the address paying the gas fee to the hot wallet came from the mixer Tornado Cash—interchange internal transfers would never use mixers for payments; this unusual detail had been flagged by independent analysts two days before the attack, yet it failed to trigger Binance's automatic circuit breaker. Third, the response speed was slower than external warnings—the public warnings from security companies and independent analysts came more than half an hour earlier than Binance's official statement, and the fatal authorization was still not revoked more than two hours after the incident, with a deposit card still en route and potentially being scanned again at any time. The defender lost three steps, while the attacker only needed to win one. The accounts are divided into three calibers: gross outflow of 5.57-6.3 billion; 3 billion+ frozen; and net loss of approximately 1 billion USD (calculated by DefiLlama founder 0xngmi, confirmed by CZ's repost, "possibly slightly higher than 1 billion, but will fully cover it"). II. How much does Binance actually make: Two conflicting "financial reports" only yield a vague result. Using this incident to discuss Binance's operational fundamentals, you'll discover an embarrassing fact: this company with an annual trading volume of 34 trillion USD does not publish financial reports. It's a private company and doesn't disclose audited financial statements. There are only two conflicting figures circulating: In March of this year, Forbes cited estimates from analysis firm Artemis, projecting revenues of $16-17 billion in both 2024 and 2025, approximately 2.5 times that of Coinbase; a few days later, CZ publicly refuted this, stating annual revenue was closer to $5 billion. The difference is three times, and both sides have motives—the former is valuing CZ's net worth, the latter is keeping a low profile. Without financial statements, you have to calculate it yourself. Let's extrapolate using publicly available data from 2025: Therefore, the actual revenue is most likely in the range of $6 billion to $11 billion. CZ's $5 billion is a conservative estimate after discounting, while Forbes' $17 billion is an optimistic estimate based on the listed price. The truth lies somewhere in between. Profitability can be compared to its only listed peer: Coinbase's 2025 revenue is $7.2 billion, net profit is $1.3 billion, and net profit margin is 18%. Binance's spot volume is about five times that of Coinbase. Even with a discounted net profit margin, its annual net profit is roughly in the range of $1.4 billion to $2.2 billion. Let's first look at the business landscape. Binance started in July 2017 with a $15 million token sale, becoming the world's largest exchange within six months. Today, it boasts 323 million registered users, a spot market share of approximately 38%, and daily spot trading volume three to five times that of its closest competitor, OKX. Its futures market advantage is even greater. It's no longer just a single exchange: spot trading, futures, Earn (financial management), Pay (payment), Launchpad, custody, the BNB Chain public blockchain ecosystem, and this year it also launched US stock and tokenized stock trading, all contained within a single super financial app. BNB Chain has a market capitalization of approximately $88 billion. BNB is both the fuel of the ecosystem and Binance's de facto equity certificate—so whenever Binance encounters problems, the drop in BNB's price reflects the market's real-time assessment of Binance. Regarding its assets, the available hard data is as follows: Custodial user assets are approximately $144 billion (based on on-chain analysis); reserve certificates show 682,000 BTC, 3.98 million ETH, and 32.3 billion USDT, with reserve ratios around 100%; the SAFU insurance fund holds 15,000 BTC, approximately $1.2 billion; compliance-related annual investments are approximately $300 million; and in March of this year, Abu Dhabi's MGX invested $2 billion, confirming the company's overall valuation at approximately $100 billion, with CZ holding about 90% of the shares, giving him a net worth of $110 billion, surpassing Bill Gates. Drawing a timeline of this company's security history makes things clearer: Over eight years, the amount stolen increased dozens of times, but the point of attack remained the same: it was never a problem with the cryptographic mathematics, but rather the engineering gap at the interface between "humans" and "automated systems." This time, even the gap was smaller—the signature system was simply tricked into signing an inappropriate document. Putting these figures back into the context of this incident gives a completely different feel: a net loss of 1 billion, which is 6% of annual revenue according to Forbes, 20% according to CZ, and 0.69% of assets under custody. The CEO of market-making giant Wintermute put it more bluntly: Binance's size is sufficient to withstand an impact three to four times the current losses. In short: it's like someone moved a truckload of gold bars from a vault, but the vault itself remained completely unscathed.

III. What saved 3 billion was precisely the "most centralized" thing

37 minutes after the incident, the largest joint interception in crypto history began.

Tether was the first to act, freezing 1.567 billion USDT; three minutes later, Circle blacklisted 823 million USDC; then Ripple froze 200 million RLUSD, World Liberty Financial (owned by the Trump family) froze 27 million USD1, Paxos froze 1,906 gold tokens, and even Arbitrum's security council intervened, locking up 30.5 million.

As of the last official confirmation from Binance, the total amount frozen has exceeded $3 billion, with an astonishing increase of $5 million per minute. This reveals a paradox, ironic yet crucial for every crypto user: what can be recovered are the most "centralized" assets. Stablecoins are debts owed to you by their issuers, who have the power to blacklist you with a single click—precisely the "centralized backdoor" that the crypto world once scorned, yet it has become the main force saving Binance. Meanwhile, the stolen native ETH and BTC, exceeding $1 billion, cannot be frozen by anyone; it's like spilled water. Decentralization protects you from censorship, but it also protects thieves from repercussions—two sides of the same coin. One more detail needs clarification: freezing is not the same as recovery. The blacklisted USDT and USDC are simply sitting still, unable to move. They will only return to Binance's account after law enforcement or the court confirms ownership, and the issuer destroys and remints them—Tether and Circle have done this before, but the process takes weeks, not hours. Therefore, the actual effect of this $3 billion freeze is to first plug the bulk of Binance's compensation gap; the actual recovery of funds will have to go through legal procedures. This is why Binance is said to "compensate first, then recover"—it's using its own money. Even the DeFi world is on edge: Aave has urgently suspended new deposits and loans in its DAO governance market (withdrawals and repayments are unaffected) to prevent stolen funds from being laundered and spreading through lending protocols. The statements from top management are also noteworthy. CEO Richard Teng used cautious language, mentioning "potential security issues and user fund security"; co-founder He Yi was the first to use the term "exploit"; CZ was the most direct—"It looks like we were indeed hacked." However, Binance's official account has never used the words "hack" or "exploit." Behind this difference in wording lies a difference in legal responsibility; this detail doesn't need excessive interpretation, but it's worth remembering. In the market, panic spread within minutes: Bitcoin fell below 78,000, reaching a low of 76,980; BNB fell by as much as 9% intraday—BNB is Binance's de facto "stock price," with the market discounting it by 14%. $1.517 billion was liquidated across the entire network in 24 hours, with 230,000 people exiting the market. Of the $629 million liquidated in the first hour, $607 million were long positions. To be fair, with the Fed's interest rate meeting imminent and the AI ​​stock sell-off continuing, a significant portion of the decline was bound to happen; the hackers simply kicked a door that was already loose. Security circles are pointing in the same direction: Blockaid's CEO believes the methods are "very similar" to last year's Bybit case, and the on-chain characteristics highly match those of North Korean hackers; SlowMist points out that the attackers' operations were actually quite crude, winning through diligent practice; Musk only left behind the statement "Everyday is Zeroday"—there are zero-day vulnerabilities every day. Before 2026 was even over, more than 230 crypto protocols had already been attacked. In September, Bitget suffered a $387 million theft, and on the same day Binance was hacked, Polymarket also lost $2.7 million due to a third-party tool being compromised. As of press time, no regulatory body worldwide has made a public statement. This silence itself is a mystery. Finally, to answer a question many haven't considered: Why didn't the market crash more severely after the largest hack in history? I see three layers of answers. First, the speed of the freeze was unprecedented—prepared within 48 hours and cleared in 40 minutes, but the issuer completed the first blockade in just 37 minutes, with someone at every link in the chain taking over. Second, the speed of the commitment was unprecedented—users waited ten years during the Mt. Gox era, and lost everything during the FTX era, but this time, from CZ to He Yi, the promise of full compensation was put on the table within an hour, and the market didn't need to guess. Third, the industry's pricing has learned to distinguish between "liquidity events" and "solvency events"—Binance can afford to compensate, so the price only reflects the panic itself, not the illusion. Seven years ago, $40 million could make the market tremble; today, $6 billion only resulted in a 5% decline. This is not numbness, but progress. IV. Able to Afford This Loss, But the Bill of Trust Has Just Arrived. In summary, my assessment of the impact can be divided into three layers. First, the financial impact: bearable, but the nature of the safety net mechanism has changed. The SAFU fund, with approximately 1.2 billion, can alone cover a net loss of just over 1 billion—this is the first time since its establishment in 2018 that it has truly taken on a payout of this magnitude. However, it should be noted that, according to official statements, the payout will be jointly borne by "SAFU and the company's own funds," meaning that the safety net has essentially shifted from a "dedicated insurance pool" to "the credit on Binance's balance sheet." Binance doesn't have audited financial statements—outsiders can't verify where the 1 billion came from, or how much is left after the withdrawal; they can only wait for the updated reserve certificate after the system is fixed. The promise is transparent, but the ledger is a black box. The second layer is a trust test: the real test is in the 48 hours after withdrawals resume. Bybit provides a reference point—it was hacked for 1.5 billion last February, ultimately recovering only 48.4 million (3.2%), but it didn't collapse because it quickly restored withdrawals and took full responsibility, clearly distinguishing between a "solvency crisis" and a "security incident." Binance's current suspension of all deposits and withdrawals is trading downtime for security, but downtime is something large users dislike the most—market makers' inventory is locked in the vault, arbitrage strategies are all suspended, and these institutions won't speak publicly, but they will express their stance through immediate transfers after the system is restored. Therefore, the net outflow data after the resumption of withdrawals will be a more honest benchmark of trust than any announcement. BNB's price movement is a real-time vote on the same issue. The third layer, regulation and structure: This "largest in history" event will almost certainly bring new rules. Binance's historical baggage is clear: in 2023, it reached a settlement totaling $4.3 billion with the US Department of Justice, CFTC, etc., CZ pleaded guilty, resigned, and served four months in prison, and was pardoned last October to return to the US business world; recently, Fortune and the Wall Street Journal also reported on the internal controversy within its compliance team regarding sanctioned funds. After each crisis, regulation only increases, never decreases. This time will be no exception, and it will come from two directions simultaneously: the stablecoin system that can freeze 3 billion in 48 hours of cold start will be repeatedly showcased by regulators—"Look how useful we are"; while a private exchange that secretly underwrote 1 billion will be required to "show its books since it can afford to pay"—the pressure to shift from "self-reporting" to "third-party auditing" for reserve certificates will be unprecedented. Looking further ahead, what truly rewrites industry perception this time is the attack itself: EIP-7702, launched just over a year ago, has been weaponized. AI has shifted the balance of power in favor of the attackers, and according to the CEO of Immunefi, it will take the defenders three to four years to catch up. Reports indicate that several leading exchanges are already vying for access to the latest security model, using AI to defend against AI. In the future, all exchanges will need to redesign their defenses against the new risk of "signature pipeline hijacking"—hardware-level secondary verification, authorization whitelists, and automatic disconnection of abnormal authorizations. These procedures, which don't exist today, will become industry standards tomorrow. The arms race between compliance and security costs has only just begun. There's also an industry-wide paradox worth considering: when a major exchange experiences a crisis, funds tend to flow to other major exchanges rather than decentralized protocols in the short term—the instinct for risk aversion is to find a "bigger safe," not "no safe." But every such event is essentially renewing the "not your keys, not your coins" policy. V. Four Things Ordinary Users Should Do Before Withdrawals Are Restored

In terms of operation, I offer four practical tips.

First, do not deposit funds into Binance before withdrawals are restored and the post-mortem report is released. The official cause (private key leak or signature system hijacking) has not yet been announced; depositing funds at this time is like pouring water into a pipe that hasn't been fully inspected.

Second, be wary of secondary scams. Every major event is followed by a wave of fake customer service and fake compensation links.

Any phone calls or private messages requesting account information or verification codes should be treated as hacking. Third, large amounts of assets should be returned to hardware wallets. The most frightening aspect of this incident is that the exchange with the most substantial security budget had its defenses breached by a single laptop. Self-custody is not a belief, it's decentralization. Fourth, monitor four indicators: ① The crucial characterization in the official review report—whether it was a private key leak or a breach of the signature pipeline—the industry consequences are completely different; ② The net outflow scale after withdrawals resume; ③ The updated reserve certificate after the repair, to see if the backstop is truly sufficient; ④ What the first regulatory agency to speak out said. Here are three conditions for disproving the claim: if the final net loss exceeds $3 billion (wiping out an entire year's profit according to Forbes); if there is a sustained large-scale run on the platform after withdrawals resume; if a major regulatory agency initiates new enforcement proceedings against Binance—if any one of these conditions is triggered, the assessment of "financially sustainable" is invalidated. Finally, a side note. In 2019, Binance was robbed of 7,000 BTC, worth $40 million. The announcement at the time included the statement: "Funds are SAFU." Seven years later, the cost of that phrase has increased 25 times, but what it represents remains unchanged—centralized exchanges never just sell trading services; they sell the promise that "I'm better able to protect your money than you are to anyone else." This incident proves that the promise remains valid, and also serves as a reminder of its price: the weight of a laptop.

data.title: How did the hackers obtain authorization to transfer approximately $6.3 billion from Binance?
data.description:
In the early hours of October 30th, Binance was suspected of being hacked, with large sums of money flowing out of multiple wallets. Approximately $6.3 billion (equivalent to about 42.064 billion RMB at the current exchange rate, though different sources have different estimates) of assets flowed out of Binance wallets across eight blockchains within about 40 minutes, with Ethereum experiencing the largest outflow. Regarding Bitcoin, 18,270 BTC were transferred out in the same block, equivalent to approximately $1.4 billion.

According to on-chain data analysis, at 4:20:59 AM Beijing time on October 30th, an Ethereum transaction was completed on the blockchain. It did not show the transfer amount or access any data; the only content was the submission of 50 EIP-7702 authorizations to the Binance hot wallet marked "Binance 14".

Three minutes and 24 seconds later, all 167,464 ETH, 1.615 billion USDT, and 63 other tokens including UNI, LINK, AAVE, and PEPE in this wallet were transferred out in a single transaction. During the same period, funds were also transferred out of Binance wallets on other blockchains.

Binance exchange stated that approximately $3 billion (approximately 20.031 billion RMB at the current exchange rate) of assets involved in the case has been frozen. Bobby Lee, founder of digital asset hardware wallet company Ballet Global, stated that only stablecoins still have a real possibility of recovery.

Q: How did the attacker launch this attack? A: On-chain records show that the attacker began preparations two days in advance. On October 28th, the attacker withdrew a small amount of ETH from Tornado Cash to pay transaction fees; on October 29th, a cleanup contract was deployed, and test tokens were used to practice the EIP-7702 authorization process. In the early morning of October 30th, the attack officially began. The attacker used the EIP-7702 authorization mechanism to have Binance 14 hot wallets delegate the execution of contracts controlled by the attacker, subsequently transferring assets from the wallets in bulk. Q: What was the key chain of this attack? A: The attack can be summarized in four steps: 1. Preparation: Attackers obtain transaction fee funds in advance through a mixer and deploy cleanup contracts and rehearse authorization processes. 2. Obtaining Authorization Signatures: By intruding into internal devices or service permissions, attackers force hot wallets to sign the EIP-7702 authorization tuple. 3. Triggering Bulk Transfers: After authorization takes effect, the hot wallet delegates the execution of contracts controlled by the attackers, transferring assets in bulk. 4. Distribution and Liquidation: Some assets are exchanged through decentralized exchanges, and some attempts are made to obtain liquidity through lending protocols. Q: How much asset transfer was caused by this attack? A: Taking the Ethereum network as an example, Binance 14 transferred out approximately 167,000 ETH and USDT worth approximately $1.615 billion, while also involving dozens of other tokens. Subsequently, other wallets such as Binance 16 also experienced abnormal transfers. The attack was not limited to Ethereum; abnormal fund transfers also occurred on multiple networks such as Bitcoin, Tron, and Solana. Q: Does $6.3 billion mean that the total loss has been confirmed? A: Not necessarily. Different research institutions have different treatments regarding the addresses involved, the scope of assets, and the statistical time points, resulting in different estimates of the on-chain transfer amount. Binance's figure of $6.3 billion is the preliminary impact of the incident, but this does not equate to a confirmed final loss of $6.3 billion. Q: How is this attack different from directly stealing private keys? A: This attack exploited the account authorization mechanism, turning wallets into tools for executing bulk transfers, rather than directly stealing private keys. The attacker exploited Ethereum's account mechanism, EIP-7702, which allows ordinary accounts to delegate smart contract code execution, enabling wallets to perform batch operations and other functions. Q: Is EIP-7702 itself a security vulnerability? A: EIP-7702 itself is not a security vulnerability. The real issue is how the attacker obtained the signature required for wallet authorization. Back in October 2024, in a discussion on the Ethereum community forum, developer 0xjustadev warned that this mechanism could allow attackers to use difficult-to-identify signatures to transfer all valuable assets in an account, including native tokens. Q: How exactly did the attacker obtain the authorization? A: Binance stated in its initial investigation that the incident may be related to the hacking of a DevOps engineer's laptop. The attacker may have used this access to the service container and submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance also stated that there is currently no evidence of wallet private key leakage, and a full technical post-incident analysis will require the investigation to conclude. Q: How many assets are currently frozen? A: According to Reuters, Tether has frozen nearly $1.57 billion in related assets, Circle has frozen over $800 million, and Ripple has frozen approximately $200 million. Binance subsequently stated that its on-chain partners have frozen approximately $3 billion in assets. Q: Have the attackers started transferring or monetizing the stolen assets? A: Yes. The attackers have sold or exchanged approximately $431 million worth of assets through decentralized exchanges, involving transactions such as exchanging altcoins and stablecoins for ETH. In addition, the attackers attempted to obtain liquidity using lending protocols, depositing approximately $60 million USDT as collateral into Aave and lending out 19,762 ETH. Such operations mean that the stolen assets may not only become market selling pressure but may also enter the on-chain lending system, creating additional risk exposure. Q: What is EIP-7702? A: EIP-7702 is an account mechanism introduced in the Ethereum Pectra upgrade. It allows ordinary external accounts to temporarily point to a deployed smart contract through a new transaction type, thereby gaining capabilities similar to smart contract accounts, such as bulk transactions, gas payment on behalf, and custom authorization. Simply put, it allows ordinary wallets to "borrow" the functionality of smart contracts for a short period without changing addresses or migrating accounts. Q: How does the authorization process occur? A: During authorization, the account owner needs to sign an authorization tuple. This tuple typically includes the chain ID, the target contract address, the nonce, and signature data used for verification. When the transaction is processed on-chain, the network verifies whether the signature comes from the account. If verification passes, the account will temporarily delegate the code of the specified contract during execution; after the transaction ends, the account usually reverts to a normal external account state. Q: Why can it achieve batch transfers? A: Because once the authorization takes effect, the account can execute operations according to the logic of the delegated contract. If an attacker controls the delegated contract, they can make the authorized account transfer tokens, ETH, or other assets in batches according to their script. In this Binance incident, the attacker used EIP-7702 to make a hot wallet delegate the execution of a contract they controlled, thereby triggering a batch transfer of assets. Q: Is EIP-7702 itself a vulnerability? A: No. EIP-7702 was designed to enhance account capabilities, not to create a backdoor. However, it introduces a new security boundary: once an account signs the authorization tuple, the delegation contract can execute operations on behalf of that account. If the signature is maliciously obtained, or the delegation target is untrustworthy, account assets could be quickly transferred. Q: How do attackers bypass the signature process? A: Public analysis shows that the problem is not that Ethereum cryptography has been broken, but rather "who initiated the authorization signature." On-chain replays show that the attacker had Binance's hot wallet sign multiple consecutive nonce EIP-7702 delegations. Due to the frequent transactions in the hot wallet, the attacker could not determine in advance which nonce would take effect, so they used a batch nonce window to increase the hit rate. Binance's initial investigation suggests the incident may be related to the compromise of a DevOps engineer's laptop. The attacker may have gained access to an internal service container and submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions. This means the attacker may not have directly obtained the plaintext private key, but may have bypassed internal signature processes, permission checks, or operational instruction pipelines, causing the system to treat dangerous authorization requests as legitimate ones. Q: Why didn't the signature system detect the anomaly? A: EIP-7702's authorized signature object is typically a digest, rather than containing complete fields such as recipient, amount, and call data as in traditional transactions. If the internal signature system only signs the 32-byte digest without analyzing whether it's a regular transaction or an EIP-7702 authorization, it's difficult to identify the risks. Once an attacker obtains a valid signature, they can temporarily execute malicious contract logic on an account. Q: What's the most alarming point? A: This incident reminds us that crypto asset security isn't just about whether the private key has been leaked. Even if the private key isn't directly stolen, if there are gaps in the signing process, operational permissions, service containers, and withdrawal approvals, attackers can still make the system "legally" execute dangerous operations. EIP-7702 amplifies this risk: it makes authorization more powerful and also makes the consequences of missigning, induced signing, and abuse of internal permissions more severe.

data.title: Binance suspected of suffering the largest hack in history, involving over $6 billion.
data.description:
Security alerts in the crypto market are becoming increasingly frequent.

Since October, from attacks on the hardware wallet supply chain to prediction platforms suspending trading due to security incidents involving third-party service providers, and then to exchanges being hacked, security risks have been constantly impacting market confidence. On October 30, Binance, one of the world's largest crypto exchanges, was also embroiled in a security incident that could break industry records.

Binance initially estimates that the incident will affect approximately $6.3 billion, with about $3 billion in assets currently frozen. If it is ultimately confirmed that all related assets have been stolen, the scale of this incident will far exceed the approximately $1.5 billion theft from Bybit in 2025, becoming one of the largest cryptocurrency thefts in recorded history.

But the key aspect of this incident isn't just the amount of money involved. Attackers used wallet authorization mechanisms to transfer assets, and stablecoin issuers such as Tether and Circle subsequently froze some funds. Meanwhile, the attacked Binance wallets also involved its publicly disclosed reserve assets. This attack has once again brought user asset reserves, exchange custody risks, and stablecoin freezing mechanisms to the forefront. $6 billion in 55 minutes. On-chain records show that the attackers began preparing for this attack two days in advance. Analysis of the relevant addresses by independent researchers shows that the attacker withdrew a small amount of ETH from Tornado Cash on October 28 to pay on-chain transaction fees; on October 29, a cleanup contract was deployed, and test tokens were used to practice the EIP-7702 authorization process. The attack officially began in the early morning of October 30. On-chain records show that the attacker first used the EIP-7702 authorization mechanism to have Binance's Binance 14 hot wallet delegate the execution of a contract controlled by the attacker. Subsequently, the contract began to transfer assets from the wallet in bulk. Taking the Ethereum network as an example, Binance 14 transferred out approximately 167,000 ETH and USDT worth approximately $1.615 billion, while also involving dozens of other tokens. Subsequently, other wallets such as Binance 16 also experienced abnormal transfers. The attack was not limited to Ethereum. Abnormal fund transfers were also observed on multiple networks including Bitcoin, Tron, and Solana. Different research institutions have different treatments regarding the addresses involved, the range of assets, and the statistical time points, resulting in different estimates of the on-chain transfer amounts. Binance's own preliminary investigation estimates the impact of the incident at approximately $6.3 billion, but this does not mean that a final loss of $6.3 billion has been confirmed. Unlike directly stealing private keys, this attack exploited the account authorization mechanism, turning the wallet into a tool for executing bulk transfers. The attacker was able to make Binance hot wallets execute bulk transfers, provided they obtained the corresponding transaction authorization. The question is, how exactly did the attacker obtain this authorization? On-chain records show that the attacker used the Ethereum account mechanism EIP-7702. This mechanism allows ordinary accounts to delegate the execution of smart contract code, enabling wallets to perform functions such as bulk operations. According to on-chain researchers, attackers exploited this mechanism to force Binance 14 to execute a contract operation that transferred assets in bulk. However, EIP-7702 itself is not a security vulnerability. The real issue lies in how the attacker obtained the signature required for wallet authorization. This risk was actually raised during the mechanism's discussion phase. In October 2024, in an EIP-7702 discussion on the Ethereum community forum, developer 0xjustadev warned that the mechanism could allow attackers to use difficult-to-identify signatures to transfer all valuable assets in an account, including native tokens. This illustrates that once ordinary accounts gain the ability to delegate smart contract execution, the security of user-signed authorizations becomes even more critical. Once an attacker obtains valid authorization, they could potentially use the delegated code to execute bulk asset transfers. Binance stated in its initial investigation that the incident may be related to the compromise of a DevOps engineer's laptop. The attacker could have used this access to the service container and submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance also stated that there is currently no evidence of wallet private key leakage, and a complete post-incident technical analysis will require further investigation. If this initial assessment is ultimately confirmed, the attack path is not merely a stolen wallet private key, but rather a breach in the security boundaries between the exchange's internal equipment, service permissions, and fund signing processes. For exchanges, protecting assets is not just about storing private keys in a secure location. Who can initiate transactions, who can call the signature service, which internal systems have access permissions, and whether abnormal operations can be intercepted in a timely manner are all part of asset custody security. After the attackers completed the asset transfer, another struggle for control of the funds ensued: stablecoin issuers began freezing related assets, while the attackers attempted to transfer funds to assets and networks that could not be directly frozen. Tether, Circle, and other issuers successively froze stablecoins related to the incident. According to Reuters, Tether froze nearly $1.57 billion in related assets, Circle froze over $800 million, and Ripple froze approximately $200 million. Binance subsequently stated that its on-chain partners had frozen approximately $3 billion in assets. PANews' real-time dashboard tracks the freezing status based on the blacklist status of USDT and USDC contracts. As of the time of the dashboard's statistics, approximately $2.579 billion in assets had been identified as frozen. This figure is not exactly the same as the approximately $3 billion announced by Binance; it mainly depends on the statistical scope and update time of both parties. However, freezing is not the same as recovery. It can only prevent specific addresses from continuing to transfer tokens controlled by the issuer. Whether the funds are ultimately returned requires further investigation and processing. Meanwhile, the attackers were also attempting to dispose of the assets through exchanges, sales, and staking. PANews reported that the attackers had sold or exchanged approximately $431 million worth of assets through decentralized exchanges, involving transactions such as exchanging altcoins and stablecoins for ETH. This means that some of the stolen assets have entered the on-chain trading market, rather than just remaining in wallets controlled by the attackers. The attackers also attempted to obtain liquidity using lending protocols. On-chain records show that the attackers deposited approximately $60 million in USDT as collateral into Aave and borrowed 19,762 ETH. This type of operation differs from directly selling assets: attackers borrow another crypto asset by pledging their existing assets, obtaining new funds while retaining the collateral position. The stolen assets may therefore not only become market selling pressure but may also enter on-chain lending systems, creating additional risk exposure. Stablecoin issuers can freeze their own USDT and USDC, but cannot freeze assets like BTC and ETH in the same way. Once the funds are converted into other crypto assets, the issuer loses this direct control. Therefore, the frozen amount does not equal the recovered amount, and one cannot simply subtract the frozen amount from the event's impact to determine how much the attacker ultimately took. Whether the funds have been exchanged, transferred across chains, sold, or used as collateral for loans will affect subsequent tracking and recovery. Whether the funds can be recovered is one aspect; whether the asset transfer affects the exchange's reserve guarantee for users is another layer of risk brought about by this incident. CoinDesk's analysis of Binance's reserve proof on October 1st found that Binance 14 was one of the reserve wallets publicly listed by Binance. At that time, the wallet held approximately 89,500 ETH and 1.26 billion USDT, among other assets. This means that the attacked wallet was not merely a temporary operational account unrelated to user assets; it had previously served as a support for the platform's reserve assets. CoinDesk estimates that the related ETH transfers may have reduced Binance's ETH reserve coverage from 100% to approximately 94%. Reserve coverage for USDC and some other tokens may also be affected. It's important to note that proof of reserves reflects asset and user liability status at a specific statistical point in time and is not equivalent to real-time asset monitoring. CoinDesk's analysis doesn't directly prove Binance is insolvent, but it raises a more specific question: when an exchange's reserve wallets supporting user balances are attacked, how quickly does the platform need to replenish its assets to maintain adequate reserves? Binance subsequently promised that all losses would be covered by the SAFU Fund and company funds, and that it would update its proof-of-reserve after the repairs were completed. This commitment means that Binance will not directly pass on the losses caused by this incident to users. However, what the market really needs to observe is the subsequent reserve data: has Binance replenished the affected assets? Are user assets still adequately supported? And can the new proof-of-reserve reflect the situation after the repairs? Frequent Security Incidents This Binance incident is not an isolated case. In recent years, Binance and its related ecosystem have experienced numerous large-scale security incidents. In May 2019, hackers obtained users' API keys and Google Authenticator codes through phishing and malware, transferring 7,000 BTC from Binance's hot wallet, worth approximately $41 million at the time. Binance subsequently used its SAFU fund to fully compensate users and suspended deposit and withdrawal services for about a week. In October 2022, the BNB Chain cross-chain bridge was attacked, with attackers using forged verification proofs to mint 2 million BNB, worth approximately $570 million. However, the latter occurred on the cross-chain bridge, not on the Binance exchange itself. From an industry-wide perspective, the impact of security incidents is also expanding. According to SlowMist, 182 security incidents occurred in the first half of 2026, resulting in approximately $956 million in losses, representing a 50.41% year-on-year increase in the number of incidents. Recent cases also involve different attack stages. Hours before the Binance incident, the prediction platform Polymarket suspended trading due to an attack on third-party service provider DebugBear. Arkham traced a suspected attacker address holding approximately $2.65 million in POL. On September 24, Bitget suffered a theft of approximately $387.5 million in assets. According to Bitget's subsequent disclosures and investigations by security agencies, attackers exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a third-party security product to obtain high-privilege internal credentials and compromised two third-party security devices, subsequently forging withdrawal instructions. Bitget stated that no wallet private keys were compromised in the incident. On-chain investigator ZachXBT discovered that the approximately $6.3 billion stolen from Binance and the approximately $388 million stolen from Bitget flowed into the same address via THORChain, subsequently resulting in the funds being mixed. ZachXBT believes that both incidents were likely carried out by the same attacker. From hot wallets and cross-chain bridges to third-party service providers and internal credentials, these incidents involve different technical paths, but they all illustrate that the security risks of crypto assets are not limited to smart contract vulnerabilities or private key leaks. Internal exchange permissions, external service providers, and on-chain fund transfer processes can all become entry points for attackers. On October 30th at noon, He Yi stated that the deposit function was operating normally, and the team was strengthening the management of withdrawal services and related addresses, expecting withdrawals to gradually resume within the next 48 hours. Binance also stated that it would release a detailed technical post-incident analysis after verifying the facts. However, the resumption of withdrawals and the freezing of funds do not mean that this incident is over. How much of the assets transferred by the attackers can be recovered, how Binance will replenish the affected reserves, and whether subsequent proof-of-reserve will show that user assets are adequately supported remain issues that the market needs to focus on.
